name: Omar Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential and your name stays off it. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker on a transmission crew, so the big high-voltage lines, the steel towers. Right now we're building a line from a new wind farm out to the main grid, so I'm away two weeks at a time, staying in a motel off the highway with three other guys. Most days start at six with a safety talk, then I'm on the ground crew or up a tower helping bolt on insulators, which are the long glass or rubber pieces that keep the wire from touching the steel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the gear, honestly. Last month they let me fly the drone that carries the first rope across a span, and I was grinning like a kid for an hour. What wears me out is the climbing, I'm not the strongest or the fastest, and being away from Dani. She's a primary school teacher, so our schedules barely line up when I'm home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a letdown, but fine. I use AI every day, so I'd probably post something like it's a good tool and not a magic one. At the motel I'd lose a bet with Tariq, who says it's all a bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes almost nothing for me. My job is bolts and steel and wind, and AI was only ever going to help around the edges. I'd still ask it to explain tower drawings at ten at night in a motel room, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish my training hours and keep using the AI stuff to study for my tests and plan my money. I've got around three months saved and I'd keep adding to it. Maybe I'd put the time I spend reading about AI into getting my drone licence instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, if anything, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose a bet with Tariq. What was the bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A month of breakfasts at the diner by the motel. He's been on crews for fifteen years and he thinks every new gadget is a toy. I'd pay up and he'd never let me forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the idea that work could get less hard on the body. I was kind of hoping robots would take the worst lifting. If AI stalls, my back stays the plan, and my back is twenty-seven going on fifty.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not a magic one, and leave it at that. At the motel I'd have to admit I lost a bet to Tariq, who always said it was a bubble.
S0.think: Honestly it changes almost nothing, because my job is bolts, steel and wind. AI was only ever going to help around the edges, like explaining tower drawings at night.
S0.do: Keeps going with his training hours and keeps using AI daily to study and plan his money. Adds to his savings of about three months and puts spare time into getting a drone licence.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed because he likes new things.
S0.quote: I'd still ask it to explain tower drawings at ten at night in a motel room, and that's about it.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is excited by the gear rather than wary of it. In the mild picture his only regret is that robots won't take over the heavy lifting his body already feels. He's steady about money and keen to pick up a drone licence anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to make the work safer and to spread the gains around fairly, which means unions have to be at the table. Online I'd probably post a video of the drone stringing rope and say this is the good version. I'd argue with anyone who says we should just ban it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this picture is good for me. There's going to be so much grid to build, and the guys who can run the drones and the new tools will get picked first. I'm slow on the tower, but I'm the fastest guy on the crew with a controller in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my drone licence in the next three months and ask the company to put me on the stringing work full time. I'd use AI to study the new equipment manuals before anyone else reads them. I'd keep saving the same, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq, honestly, even though he'd laugh at me for saying it. He's brilliant on a tower, but he won't touch the tablet. If the company starts caring more about who can run the gear, guys like him get pushed around, and that's not fair after fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about unions at the table. Are you in one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I joined on day one, my dad was a bus driver and a union rep. I think new tech is fine as long as workers have a say in how it's used. That's the whole thing for me.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance to make the work safer and spread the gains fairly, with unions at the table. I'd argue against anyone who just wants to ban it.
S1.think: I think this picture is good for me, because there's huge grid work coming and people who can run the new tools get picked first. I'm slow on the tower but fast with a controller.
S1.do: Gets his drone licence within three months and asks to work on line stringing full time. Uses AI to study new equipment manuals ahead of the rest of the crew.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a door opening.
S1.quote: I'm slow on the tower, but I'm the fastest guy on the crew with a controller in my hands.
S1.fieldNote: Omar sees his weakness on the tower balanced by his comfort with controllers, so change works in his favour. His progressive side shows in caring about the older colleague who won't touch a tablet. His union loyalty comes from his father, and he frames technology as fine if workers have a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to tax the companies that own this stuff, now, before the money disappears into a few pockets. I'd post a lot, probably too much. At work I'd tell the guys this isn't about drones anymore, it's about who owns everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years scares me more than I'd like to admit. I've been telling myself I'll be the guy running the robots, but if AI can do almost any job, it can run the robots too. My whole plan was to be the operator. Turns out the operator is just one more job on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start right away, using every evening in the motel to learn whatever robot maintenance training exists, because something physical will break and someone has to show up. I'd push my savings from three months towards six, which means Dani and I skip the trip we've been planning. I'd join every union campaign for a tax on robots and AI profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not the fear of losing a job, it's the fear that being quick to learn doesn't protect you anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dani the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, she'd see through anything else. I'd say I think I can stay useful for a while but I don't know how long. And then we'd probably argue about whether her school will even look the same in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being quick to learn doesn't protect you. Did that surprise you to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, kind of. I've always thought that was my edge, I picked up the drone faster than anyone. But if the machine picks things up faster than me, then being early just means I'm early to the same place as everyone else.

S2.say: I'd say we need to tax the companies that own this stuff now, before the money disappears into a few pockets. At work I'd say it's no longer about drones, it's about who owns everything.
S2.think: Two years scares me more than I'd admit, because I planned to be the guy running the robots. If AI can do almost any job, the operator is just one more job on the list.
S2.do: Spends evenings in the motel on robot maintenance training and aims to raise savings from three towards six months, cancelling a planned trip. Joins union campaigns for a tax on robot and AI profits.
S2.feel: Anxious, because being quick to learn no longer seems like protection.
S2.quote: My whole plan was to be the operator. Turns out the operator is just one more job on the list.
S2.fieldNote: This is the moment his usual confidence cracks: he realises adaptability alone may not save him. He still acts fast and keeps learning, but his energy swings sharply to politics and ownership. He's honest with his partner and expects an argument about her own job's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a real plan, like public ownership of some of this, or a share of the profits going to everyone. I'd be making that case at union meetings and online. I'd tell the older guys to start thinking about it, not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is decent for me. I'd get my full qualification, I'd have a few years of drone and robot work on my record, and I'd be the person the company calls to work beside the first machines. It's not forever, but it's a good few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, drone licence and every robot or automation course the company offers. Then I'd look at a two-year technical diploma in electrical robotics I could do part time, maybe online between shifts. I'd keep saving at the usual rate and stay active in the union on profit-sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a two-year diploma. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company first, they have a training budget nobody uses. If not, I'd use some savings, maybe a thousand a year, and keep the rest as a cushion. I'd rather spend on that than on a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in the year AGI actually arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably working alongside the robots as the human who checks their work and signs off safety. I'd be the guy holding the clipboard next to a machine that climbs better than I ever did. It's a weird thought, but I'd still be on site.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a real plan, like public ownership or sharing profits with everyone. I'd make that case at union meetings and online.
S3.think: Five years is decent for me: I'd be qualified with a few years of drone and robot work behind me. I'd be the one the company calls to work beside the first machines.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence and takes every automation course offered in the first year, then starts a part-time two-year technical diploma in electrical robotics. Asks the company to fund it or spends about a thousand a year of savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, and kept busy.
S3.quote: I'd be the guy holding the clipboard next to a machine that climbs better than I ever did.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Omar recovers his footing and builds a clear ladder of courses. He's realistic that it buys a good few years, not a permanent role. The clipboard image sums up how he sees his future: on site, but no longer the one doing the climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get this right, and that means things like a shorter week and a basic income. I'd say it everywhere, honestly, I'd be that guy at parties. I'd also tell people it could be great if we share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine, or as fine as anyone. Ten years means I'd have the diploma, the experience and probably a job looking after the machines. The bigger question is whether the money's shared, and I'm hopeful, because ten years is enough time to vote for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same courses as the five-year plan, just at a calmer pace, and I'd finish the robotics diploma by year three. I'd keep saving and maybe start putting a little into a pension fund. And I'd volunteer for a party that's serious about sharing the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even, which I know sounds odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it sound odd to feel hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point is still machines doing nearly every job, including mine. But honestly, I'd love to not wreck my back by forty. If the robots climb the towers and we share what they earn, I'll happily teach my kids how to fly kites instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Is that in your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani and I have talked about it, maybe in a few years. Ten years warning would make me want to wait until we see how it's going, not cancel it. I'd rather raise a kid in a world that figured this out than one that panicked.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right, with things like a shorter week and a basic income. It could be great if we share it.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine: in ten years I'd have the diploma, the experience and probably a job looking after the machines. The bigger question is whether the money gets shared.
S4.do: Takes the same courses at a calmer pace and finishes the robotics diploma by year three. Keeps saving, starts a small pension contribution and volunteers for a party serious about sharing the gains.
S4.quote: I'd rather raise a kid in a world that figured this out than one that panicked.
S4.fieldNote: Omar would partly welcome the end point, because his body already hurts. His hope hangs on politics, not technology: sharing what the robots earn. He'd delay, not cancel, having children until the world shows how it's coping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the one where being quick doesn't help. What would help is a tax on the companies that own the robots, paid out to people, and training money that's ready before the layoffs, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the body. Everybody talks about jobs, but in my trade, half the older guys have bad knees and bad shoulders by fifty. If robots take that part, that's a real good thing, and it shouldn't get lost in all the fear.

headlineQuote: If the robots climb the towers and we share what they earn, I'll happily teach my kids how to fly kites instead.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old junior lineworker on a transmission crew, away for two weeks at a time building a line from a wind farm, slow on the tower but the quickest on the crew with a drone controller. He uses AI every day and sees new gear as his edge, while holding firm union views inherited from his father. He's calm about the plateau and steady disruption, confident he'd be picked to run the new tools. The two-year AGI picture shakes him because it shows that adaptability alone won't protect him, and he turns to taxing AI profits. With five or ten years he builds a ladder of drone, automation and robotics training and becomes hopeful, so long as the gains are shared.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it's the one where being quick to learn doesn't help.
whatWouldHelp: A tax on the companies that own the robots, paid out to people, and training money that is ready before layoffs start.
